title: Strings, parameter expansion and dates
goal: Cut and change text inside variables without extra tools, and make correct dates and file names for backups and releases.
setup: printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Usage: release-name.sh <archive-path> <build-date>' '# Prints:' '#   name:    todo-api-2.4.1   (file name without .tar.gz)' '#   tag:     2-4-1            (version, every dot changed to a dash)' '#   date:    2026-10-20       (build date as YYYY-MM-DD)' '#   workdir: a NEW empty folder, also when the script runs twice' 'FILE=${1##*/}' 'NAME=${FILE%.*}' 'VERSION=${NAME#todo-api-}' 'TAG=${VERSION/./-}' 'BUILD_DATE=$(date -d "$2" +%d-%m-%Y)' 'WORKDIR=release-work' 'mkdir $WORKDIR' 'echo "name:    $NAME"' 'echo "tag:     $TAG"' 'echo "date:    $BUILD_DATE"' 'echo "workdir: $WORKDIR"' > release-name.sh

warmup.q: Which pipeline gives the top 10 IPs of an access log?
How do you find `.log` files older than 7 days under `/var/log`?
How do you replace `8080` with `9090` in a file and keep a backup?
Why must find patterns like `*.log` be quoted?
warmup.a: Without quotes, bash may expand `*.log` to file names in the current folder before find runs.

problems.title: Path surgery: ##*/ %/* %.ext, basename, dirname
problems.situation: A CI job gets the artifact path `/opt/releases/todo-api-2.4.1.tar.gz`. The deploy step needs the file name, the folder, the name without `.tar.gz`, and the version `2.4.1`. Parameter expansion does this inside bash, with no extra programs.
task: Set `ARTIFACT=/opt/releases/todo-api-2.4.1.tar.gz`.
Print the file name with `${ARTIFACT##*/}` and the folder with `${ARTIFACT%/*}`.
Print the name without `.tar.gz` with `%.tar.gz`. Then try `%.*` and `%%.*` and compare.
Get only the version `2.4.1`: remove the prefix `todo-api-` with `#`, then the suffix.
Do the same file name and folder with `basename` and `dirname`.
hints: `#` removes from the start, `%` removes from the end. One sign = shortest match, two signs = longest match.
`##*/` = remove everything up to the last `/`. `%/*` = remove the last `/` and what follows.
`%.*` removes only `.gz`; `%%.*` removes from the FIRST dot, so it cuts the version too.
solution: FILE=${ARTIFACT##*/}               # remove the longest match of */ from the start
echo "folder:   ${ARTIFACT%/*}"     # remove the shortest match of /* from the end
echo "%%.*:     ${FILE%%.*}"        # longest: everything from the first dot

explanation.meaning: Remove the shortest / longest match from the START.
Remove the shortest / longest match from the END.
Everything up to the last slash is removed: the file name.
The last slash and the name are removed: the folder.
Longest match of `.*` from the end starts at the first dot: `todo-api-2`. A common bug with versions.
External commands that do the same; `basename` can also remove a suffix.

problems.expected_output:
file:     todo-api-2.4.1.tar.gz
folder:   /opt/releases
no ext:   todo-api-2.4.1
%.*:      todo-api-2.4.1.tar
%%.*:     todo-api-2
version:  2.4.1
basename: todo-api-2.4.1
dirname:  /opt/releases
mistakes: Using `${FILE%%.*}` to remove the extension of a versioned file: the result is `todo-api-2`, not `todo-api-2.4.1`.
problems.interview_say: I use `${path##*/}` for the file name and `${path%/*}` for the folder. `#` cuts from the start and `%` from the end; doubling the sign makes the match as long as possible.
problems.try_yourself: Set `URL=https://github.com/wicky/todo.git` and print only `todo` using two expansions.

problems.title: Defaults and checks: :- := :? :+ and ${#var}
problems.situation: A container entrypoint reads its settings from environment variables. Some are optional (use a default), one is required (stop if missing), and the database password must be at least 12 characters long.
task: With `PORT` unset, predict and print `${PORT:-8080}`. Is `PORT` set afterwards?
Now print `${PORT:=8080}`. Is `PORT` set afterwards?
Set `DEBUG=1` and print `${DEBUG:+--verbose}`. Then unset it and print again.
Set `DB_PASSWORD=short` and check its length with `${#DB_PASSWORD}`.
In a subshell, run `echo "${DB_HOST:?DB_HOST must be set}"` and read the error.
hints: `:-` uses a default but does not change the variable. `:=` uses it AND saves it.
`:+` gives the alternative text only when the variable IS set and not empty.
`:?` stops with the message when the variable is empty or unset.
solution: ( echo "${DB_HOST:?DB_HOST must be set}" ) || echo "exit code: $?"

explanation.meaning: Use the default when VAR is unset or empty. VAR does not change.
Same, but also assign the default to VAR.
Give `text` only if VAR has a value. Good for optional flags.
Stop with the message if VAR is unset or empty.
Length of the value in characters.

problems.expected_output:
port: 8080, PORT is now: []
port: 8080, PORT is now: [8080]
flags: [--verbose]
flags: []
password length: 5
password too short (need 12+)
bash: DB_HOST: DB_HOST must be set
exit code: 1
mistakes: Writing `${PORT-8080}` (no colon): it uses the default only when PORT is unset, not when it is empty (`PORT=`).
Using `:=` on a positional parameter: `${1:=x}` gives `$1: cannot assign in this way`.
problems.interview_say: In entrypoint scripts I use `${VAR:-default}` for optional settings, `${VAR:?message}` for required ones, and `${#VAR}` to check lengths.
problems.try_yourself: Run `bash -c 'echo ${1:=x}'` and read the error. Why can't you assign to `$1`?

problems.title: Dates for backups and releases
problems.situation: Backup files need sortable names like `db-20261020-1430.sql.gz`, a cleanup job needs the date 7 days ago, and a report needs the number of days between two dates. Here the dates are fixed with `date -d`, so the output is the same on every machine.
task: Print `2026-10-20 14:30` as `%F` (YYYY-MM-DD) and as `%Y%m%d-%H%M`.
Build the backup name `db-<stamp>.sql.gz` from that time.
Print the date 7 days before and 30 days after `2026-10-20`.
Convert the date to seconds since 1970 (`+%s`) in UTC, and back with `@seconds`.
Compute the days between `2026-10-01` and `2026-10-20`.
hints: `date -d 'TEXT' +FORMAT` reads a date from text. Without `-d`, it uses now.
`%F` = `%Y-%m-%d`. `%H%M` = hours and minutes. `%s` = epoch seconds.
Days between: `(( (end - start) / 86400 ))`, where 86400 = seconds per day.

explanation.meaning: Format a given date. `%F` = 2026-10-20 (ISO, sorts correctly).
20261020-1430: good for file names (no spaces, no colons).
Date math with words: `-7 days`, `+30 days`, `yesterday`, `next monday`.
Seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC (epoch), and back.
Use UTC for this command only, so the result does not depend on the machine's time zone.
Seconds in a day: 24 × 60 × 60.

problems.output_note: `date` without `-d` prints the current time, which is different every run. Here every date is fixed.
mistakes: Using `%d-%m-%Y` in file names: `20-10-2026` does not sort by date. Use `%F` or `%Y%m%d`.
Using `:` in file names (`%T`): Windows tools and some copies fail on colons.
`date -d` is GNU (Linux). On macOS it is `date -v-7d`. Scripts for both need care.
problems.interview_say: For backup names I use `date +%Y%m%d-%H%M` so files sort by time, `date -d '-7 days' +%F` for cleanup dates, and epoch seconds `+%s` to compute differences.
problems.try_yourself: Print today's date in Sri Lanka and in UTC: `TZ=Asia/Colombo date` and `TZ=UTC date`. How many hours apart are they?

problems.title: Clean reports with printf, and read -p
problems.situation: A status script prints a table of services for the on-call engineer, and an install script asks the user which environment to use. `echo` is fine for simple text; `printf` gives exact columns, padding and numbers.
task: Print a header and 3 rows with `printf '%-14s %6s %8s\n'` (service, port, status).
Print a number with leading zeros (`%05d`) and a percent with one decimal (`%.1f%%`).
Print every item of an array on its own line with `printf '%s\n' "${ARR[@]}"`.
Ask for the environment with `read -r -p "Environment: " ENV`. Here the answer comes from `<<< staging`, so no prompt is shown.
hints: `%-14s` = text, left aligned, 14 wide. `%6s` = right aligned, 6 wide.
printf does not add a new line: always end the format with `\n`.
`read -p` shows the prompt only when input comes from a keyboard (a terminal).
solution: printf '%-14s %6d %8s\n' todo-frontend 80 up todo-backend 8080 up postgres 5432 down

explanation.meaning: The format is reused for extra arguments: 3 rows from one format.
Left-aligned text in 14 columns / number right-aligned in 6.
Pad with zeros to 5 digits: 00042.
One decimal, then a real `%` (written `%%`).
Show a prompt, read a line into VAR. Add `-s` to hide typing (passwords).

problems.expected_output:
SERVICE          PORT   STATUS
todo-frontend      80       up
todo-backend     8080       up
postgres         5432     down
build: 00042
cpu: 87.5%
web-01
web-02
db 01
you chose: staging
mistakes: Forgetting `\n`: all output is on one line, and the prompt appears at the end.
Using `printf "$TEXT"` with user text: a `%` in the text breaks the output. Use `printf '%s\n' "$TEXT"`.
Asking for input in a CI job: there is no keyboard, so `read` gets nothing. Use arguments or environment variables there.
problems.interview_say: I use `printf` for aligned tables and exact number formats, and always `printf '%s\n' "$var"` for user text. In CI there is no keyboard, so scripts take options, not `read`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `read -r -s -p "Password: " PW; echo; echo "length: ${#PW}"` in your terminal. The typing is hidden.

problems.title: Find the bug: the release name script
problems.situation: `release-name.sh` prints the release name, tag, date and a work folder for the CI job. The output is wrong in three places, and the second run of the job fails. The goal is in the comments.
task: Run `bash release-name.sh /opt/releases/todo-api-2.4.1.tar.gz 2026-10-20` twice. Compare with the comments.
Find 4 bugs: the extension removal, the dot replacement, the date format, and the work folder.
Fix them. The work folder must be new and unique each run: use `mktemp -d`.
Run the fixed script twice.
hints: `%.*` removes only `.gz`. Remove `.tar.gz` exactly.
`${VERSION/./-}` replaces only the first dot. `//` replaces all.
`%F` gives YYYY-MM-DD. `mktemp -d` makes a new folder with a random name and prints its path.
solution: WORKDIR=$(mktemp -d)                 # new, unique folder every run
rmdir "$WORKDIR"                     # clean up our empty folder

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: `%.*` removed only `.gz` and left `todo-api-2.4.1.tar`.
Bug 2: one `/` replaces the first match; `//` replaces all.
Bug 4: a fixed folder name made the second run fail with `File exists`. mktemp makes a new unique folder.

problems.expected_output:
name:    todo-api-2.4.1.tar
tag:     2-4.1.tar
date:    20-10-2026
workdir: release-work
mkdir: cannot create directory ‘release-work’: File exists
name:    todo-api-2.4.1.tar
tag:     2-4.1.tar
date:    20-10-2026
workdir: release-work
--- fixed ---
name:    todo-api-2.4.1
tag:     2-4-1
date:    2026-10-20
workdir: created (a new folder under /tmp)
name:    todo-api-2.4.1
tag:     2-4-1
date:    2026-10-20
workdir: created (a new folder under /tmp)
problems.output_note: The broken script creates a folder `release-work` in day13. The user can delete it with `rmdir release-work`.
mistakes: Fixing bug 4 with `mkdir -p`: the second run then reuses the old folder with old files inside. CI jobs need a clean folder.
Printing the mktemp path in a test that compares output: the random name changes every run.
problems.interview_say: I remove known extensions exactly with `%`, replace all matches with `//`, use ISO dates with `%F`, and create work folders with `mktemp -d` so every run starts clean.
problems.try_yourself: Add a line that prints the tag in upper case with `${TAG^^}` and the first 3 letters of the name with `${NAME:0:3}`.

problems.title: Safe temp files: mktemp and cleanup
problems.situation: A script downloads a file, edits it, and moves it into place. Using a fixed name like `/tmp/data.json` is dangerous: two runs clash, and other users may read or replace it. `mktemp` makes a unique, private file.
task: Create a temp file with `TMP=$(mktemp)` and check its permissions with `stat -c '%a'`.
Create a temp file with a name pattern: `mktemp /tmp/todo-backup.XXXXXX`.
Write to the file, read it, and remove it at the end.
Use `trap 'rm -f "$TMP"' EXIT` in a small `bash -c` script, and show that the file is gone after the script ends.
hints: `mktemp` creates the file with permission 600 (only the owner).
`XXXXXX` in the pattern is replaced by random characters.
`trap ... EXIT` runs when the script ends, even after an error (Day 22).
solution: LEFT=$(bash -c 'T=$(mktemp); trap "rm -f \"$T\"" EXIT; echo data > "$T"; echo "$T"')
[ -e "$LEFT" ] && echo "file still there" || echo "trap removed the temp file"

explanation.meaning: Make a new empty file with a unique name under /tmp, permission 600. Prints the path.
Replaced by random letters and digits.
Run cleanup when the script exits, success or error.
A pattern: exactly 6 characters. The real name is random, so the test checks only the shape.

problems.expected_output:
permission: 600
named temp file created
{"ok": true}
trap removed the temp file
mistakes: Writing `TMP=/tmp/data.$$`: the name is guessable, so another user could create it first.
Forgetting cleanup: `/tmp` fills with old files from every run.
problems.interview_say: I create temp files with `mktemp`, which gives a unique private file, and remove them with `trap 'rm -f "$TMP"' EXIT` so they are cleaned even when the script fails.
problems.try_yourself: Run `mktemp -d` twice and compare the two names.

problems.title: More string tricks: case, substrings, replace
problems.situation: Small string jobs come up all the time in pipelines: a short git SHA for an image tag, an environment name in upper or lower case, removing spaces from a branch name, and replacing a word.
task: From `SHA=a3f9c1e7d2b4c5f6`, print the first 7 characters with `${SHA:0:7}`.
Print `ENV=Staging` in upper case `${ENV^^}` and lower case `${ENV,,}`.
Turn `feature/Add login page` into a Docker-safe tag: lower case, `/` and spaces replaced by `-`.
Replace `http://` with `https://` in a URL using `${URL/http:/https:}`.
hints: `${var:offset:length}` = substring.
`^^` = all upper case, `,,` = all lower case (bash 4+).
`${B//[\/ ]/-}` replaces every `/` or space with `-`.

explanation.meaning: 7 characters starting at position 0.
Upper / lower case.
Replace every character that is `/` or a space with `-`.
Replace the first match of `a` with `b`.

problems.expected_output:
short sha: a3f9c1e
STAGING staging
image tag: todo-api:feature-add-login-page
https://todo.example.com/api
mistakes: Using `^^` in `sh` or very old bash (macOS bash 3.2): `bad substitution`. Use `tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'` there.
Docker tags cannot contain `/` or spaces or upper case letters: `invalid reference format`.
problems.interview_say: For image tags I use `${SHA:0:7}` for a short commit id and clean branch names with `${b,,}` and `${b//\//-}`, all inside bash without extra tools.
problems.try_yourself: Remove all digits from `todo-api-2.4.1` with `${NAME//[0-9]/}`. What is left?

interview.q: How do you get the file name from a full path in bash, without basename?
What is the difference between `${VAR:-x}` and `${VAR:=x}`?
interview.a: Both give `x` when VAR is empty or unset. `:=` also saves `x` into VAR; `:-` does not change VAR.

interview.q: How do you create a timestamped backup file name?
How do you get the date 7 days ago in a script?
Why use `mktemp` instead of a fixed temp file name?
interview.a: mktemp makes a unique file with permission 600. Fixed names clash between runs and can be attacked by other users.
